281 - Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone: Cannabis sits in an odd cultural spot: illegal for decades, medically prescribed, endlessly joked about, and used by millions. This essay collection takes the plant seriously, asking whether drug-induced 'insights' are knowledge or self-induced delusion, what words like 'buzz,' 'high' and 'stoned' actually mean, whether intoxication erodes freedom and agency, and whether all use is really self-medication against a hard life. Philosophers from Plato and the Stoics to Freud and Lao Tzu weigh in.
282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone: Mountain climbing looks pointless from below, which is why George Mallory's answer to 'Why climb Everest?' — 'Because it's there' — became famous. This essay collection takes that non-answer seriously, asking why people risk death for summits, whether free soloing is sane or selfish, what kind of freedom a climber feels when options vanish, and whether such risks can be justified to grieving families. Stoics, Aristotle, Mill and Zen Buddhism all find footing on the mountain.
283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone: Tattoos have traveled from sailors, convicts, and carnival sideshows to mainstream fashion — roughly forty percent of younger Americans now wear ink. That shift makes them philosophically rich: is a tattoo art when its canvas is a living, aging person, and who decides? What does permanently marking your skin claim about identity and the self? This collection pits Descartes, Kant, and feminist aesthetics against the mirror of the tattoo parlor, taking skin seriously as a philosophical surface.
284 - College Sex – Philosophy for Every: College is where many people first navigate sex without supervision: hook-ups, friends with benefits, long-distance Skype relationships, and the occasional scandal. This essay collection treats campus romance as a serious philosophical testing ground. Can you experiment your way to becoming a wiser lover, Socrates-style? Is there an ethical way to have sex with a professor? Does selling eggs or appearing on a webcam to pay tuition violate your dignity? Aristotle, Epicurus, and Kant all turn up on campus.
285 - Serial Killers – Philosophy for Ev: True crime is a cultural obsession, and the serial killer its darkest star. This collection asks what these killers actually teach us about morality: how the Zodiac's letters turned an entire region into hunted objects, whether a psychopath can be profoundly evil yet not responsible for it, whether jurors contaminated by disgust and publicity can truly know guilt, and whether Dexter Morgan, television's vigilante killer of killers, deserves praise. Sartre, Nietzsche, Kant, and Rawls are enlisted for the grim work.
286 - Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - B: Yoga is practiced by millions as exercise, yet it grew from ancient Indian philosophy — Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, Vedanta, and Tantra — whose central promise is freedom of the self. This collection asks what 'union of mind and body' can mean if Cartesian dualism is false, whether yoga counts as an empirical 'spiritual science' compatible with skepticism, why a once-male discipline became a predominantly female pursuit, and whether stretching can survive as spirituality without the metaphysics.
287 - Blues – Philosophy for Everyone -: The blues grew out of the African-American experience of slavery, sharecropping, and Jim Crow, and became the root of nearly all popular music. It is also a philosophical puzzle: no definition of the form survives its counterexamples, so what makes a song a blues? Can a white musician authentically play it? Do recordings preserve a performer's soul or lose it? And why does singing about feeling low affirm life? Wittgenstein, Plato, and Nietzsche help think it through.
288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone -: Everyone dates, or watches others do it badly, yet the ritual is rarely examined. This collection does: What exactly is flirting, and can you do it with a chatbot? Is unconditional love an ideal or a disaster — would you still want a partner whose love survived discovering you were a murderer? Can game theory improve the search for a mate? Aristotle's ethics, decision theory, and focus groups with conservative Christian men all weigh in on romance.
289 - Horror and Philosophy - Essays on: Horror is usually dismissed as cheap thrills, but this scholarly collection argues it does real philosophical work across film, television, and literature. Psycho and The Birds dramatize radical skepticism — can you trust the ordinary person beside you? Saw and Hostel probe whether torture can ever be justified and why we enjoy watching. Land of the Dead runs Marx through the zombie apocalypse, and Angel asks what makes a vampire with a soul the same person. Horror, it turns out, is epistemology and ethics with the lights off.
297 - The Philosopher at the End of the: Mark Rowlands believes lowbrow science fiction films are among the best philosophy teachers available. This book walks through familiar blockbusters — The Matrix, The Terminator, Total Recall, Minority Report, Blade Runner, Star Wars — and shows each one staging a classic philosophical problem: Descartes' skeptical demon, the mind–body puzzle, personal identity and cloned memories, free will versus determinism, the meaning of an assembled, thrown-into-the-world life. His running claim is that philosophy is something you do, not something you know — and watching is a way of doing it.
